# Hye Vem

Build browser applications with independently installable data and interface packages.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/


Hye Vem brings shared application behavior and a consistent interface into reusable packages. Start with either package, or use them together.

| Package | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| [Vem Data](https://hyevem.com/docs/data) | Share knowledge between screens, plan backend reads, coordinate commands, and protect drafts. |
| [Vem UI](https://hyevem.com/docs/ui) | Build controls, application navigation, and feedback with a consistent design. |

## See them work together

[Explore the task board](https://hyevem.com/docs/task-board): find a task, complete it, and edit its notes. Vem UI supplies the controls. Vem Data keeps the information and actions coordinated.

## Choose your next step

- **Building a screen?** Start with [UI components](https://hyevem.com/docs/ui/components) and [displaying data](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/display).
- **Connecting a service?** Define its resources in [Connect your data](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect).
- **Matching your application?** Set [branding and appearance](https://hyevem.com/docs/ui/customize).
- **Looking up an API?** Open the [Data reference](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/reference) or [UI reference](https://hyevem.com/docs/ui/reference).


---

# Vem Data

Describe the information and operations a feature needs. Let shared infrastructure coordinate them.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data



Vem Data is independently consumable as `@hyecompany/vem-data`. A feature uses named descriptions and shared React hooks; a backend adapter supplies identity, evidence, and operation semantics.

| Learn or do | Start with |
| --- | --- |
| First application | [Start here](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/start) |
| Lists, actions, editors, and feature tests | [Build with Vem](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build) |
| Domain definitions, events, and the browser host | [Connect your data](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect) |
| Acquisition, access, and recovery | [Understand Vem](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand) |
| Exact signatures and diagnosis | [Reference and troubleshooting](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/reference) |

You can start at any recipe. Each guide names its prerequisites and links the deeper behavior it relies on.

# What Vem Data does

Keep related views up to date without coordinating them in every component.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/start/overview


Imagine a task list, a progress summary, and a notes editor. Completing a task should update both the list and the summary. Opening its details should reuse what is already known. A teammate's update should not erase the notes you are typing.

Vem Data manages that shared information. Components describe what they need; one backend integration teaches Vem where the information comes from and what changes mean.

**[Explore the task board →](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/start/quickstart)**

## What you write

For a feature, you write a query, command binding, or edit binding and render the result. You keep control of the components, layout, and validation.

For a new backend, you write its **domain definition**: how to identify resources, translate responses, handle changes, and report operation outcomes. The browser host connects that definition to shared ownership and events. Those are integration tasks, done once for many features.

## When it fits

Vem is useful when features share information, work outlives a screen, or access can change while the application is open. It includes React hooks and an imperative API and can be consumed independently of other Hye Vem packages.

For one isolated request, the integration may be more than you need. Vem does not supply a backend or decide who is authorized; it applies the rules and evidence your integration provides.

## Choose your path

| You want to… | Start with… |
| --- | --- |
| Build a screen or add a button | [Build with Vem](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build) |
| Connect your backend | [Define a resource](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/resources) |
| Understand why a read happens | [Shared knowledge](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand/acquisition) |
| Look up an API or diagnose a problem | [Reference and troubleshooting](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/reference) |

# Explore the task board

Filter a list, finish a task, and keep an edit safe.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/start/quickstart


You’re planning a weekend with a friend. Use the small app below, then see what Vem did for you. Each part starts with one thing to try.

### Explore the task board

Vem UI controls and Vem Data power three short interactions: filtering, completing a task, and editing notes. Filtering and an overview share known task data. A command previews completion until its response is known. An edit keeps its draft when a teammate changes the saved note. Each lesson runs the real Vem runtime with a simulated in-page service. Source reads are simulated calls, not HTTP. The application has no SharedWorker or browser persistence.

## What you just used

- **A query** asks for the task information a view needs. Filtering reuses what is already known.
- **A command** asks to complete a task. Its **action** keeps track of progress and the result.
- **An edit session** keeps your draft and the saved version it came from together.

These are the [four concepts](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/start/concepts) used throughout Vem. You do not need to manage requests or subscriptions in a feature component.

## The query behind the list

The task list asks for two fields and an optional filter. The component keeps `openOnly` as ordinary React state:


```tsx
const result = useQuery(
	tasks.list({
		select: ["title", "status"],
		where: openOnly ? { status: "open" } : undefined,
	}),
);
```


To build your own feature, continue to [display data](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/display), [add an action](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/actions), or [build an editor](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/editors). Each guide connects a behavior in the app to the code responsible for it.

<details>
<summary>Where the application ends and the integration begins</summary>

### Three responsibilities

1. Describe what the view needs. Render it with public hooks.
2. Define how backend responses, permissions, and operations work.
3. Connect tabs to one owner, with events and optional storage.

The tab holds a read model for synchronous rendering. The SharedWorker owns acquisition and mutation. Pure read definitions run in both places; credentials and HTTP stay in the owner integration.

The examples use Vem’s real runtime with a simulated task service. To connect your application, start with [defining a resource](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/resources). The [browser-host guide](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/browser-host) shows how to share it between tabs.

</details>


---

# Four concepts

Connect the task-board interactions to the code you write.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/start/concepts


The task board uses four concepts. Each corresponds to one ordinary piece of feature code.

| Concept | In the app | In your code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Query** | Show the unfinished tasks | `useQuery(tasks.list(...))` |
| **Command** | Ask to complete this task | `useCommand(tasks.commands.complete(target))` |
| **Action** | Track that attempt's progress and result | `useAction(handle)` |
| **Edit session** | Change notes while keeping a protected draft | `useEdit(tasks.edits.notes(target))` |

A command is a description of intended work. Calling its bound `run()` creates an action: the shared record of that particular attempt.

## Descriptions are values

Calling `tasks.list(...)` or `tasks.commands.complete(...)` alone does not read or change anything. The hook or client uses that description to request information or execute work.

Equivalent inline descriptions work without manual memoization. A new JavaScript object with the same query values is the same information request.

## Where does `tasks` come from?

It is a small contract shared by your features and backend integration. It names the available fields, commands, and edits:


```ts
import {
	defineCommand,
	defineEdit,
	defineResource,
} from "@hyecompany/vem-data";

export interface Task {
	title: string;
	status: "open" | "done";
	notes: string;
}
export interface TaskRef {
	id: string;
}
export interface Notes {
	notes: string;
}
export const tasks = defineResource<Task, TaskRef>()({
	name: "tasks",
	fields: ["title", "status", "notes"],
	defaultSelect: ["title", "status"],
	commands: { complete: defineCommand<void, { kind: "succeeded" }>() },
	edits: { notes: defineEdit<Notes, { kind: "succeeded" }>() },
});
```


The integration supplies how those names work. A feature contributor imports `tasks`; they do not repeat the definition or implement its networking. The **resource reference** `TaskRef` identifies a task, while `Task` describes its fields.

`defineCommand` and `defineEdit` also describe their input and supported outcomes. Even a contract with only `succeeded` can return a framework failure or an unknown result, so the UI still handles both.

## A query result can be useful before it is complete

A known task without its title can still appear with a placeholder. A task without its status cannot yet be placed in a “To do” filter. An empty array can mean “not known yet,” so use `result.empty` to say “No tasks.”

You can build the ordinary view first using [Display data](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/display). The [partial-results guide](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/partial-results) explains the additional states when you need them.


---

# Build with Vem

Recipes for screens, actions, editors, and tests.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build


These guides are for adding features to an application that already uses Vem. Import the application's resource contract and use the shared hooks; the application supplies the provider.

| You want to… | Start here |
| --- | --- |
| Show a list, add a column, or open a detail | [Display data](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/display) |
| Keep useful content visible during incomplete reads | [Partial results](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/partial-results) |
| Add a button with progress and outcome feedback | [Commands and actions](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/actions) |
| Edit values without losing a draft | [Protected editors](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/editors) |
| Read or run outside React | [Imperative usage](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/imperative) |
| Reproduce a feature's loading or failure states | [Feature tests](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/testing) |

New to the concepts? [Use the task board](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/start/quickstart) first. Connecting Vem to a new backend? [Define a resource](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/resources) before wiring a screen.

Feature components do not choose endpoints, maintain cache keys, or track backend operations. Those decisions are shared by the domain and host.

# Display data

Add a list, column, filter, or detail view through a typed query.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/display


Try filtering a task list and opening its notes. The component below uses the same query pattern.

### Experiment: Filter without fetching

Choose To do, open the overview, then open the walk’s notes.

Filtering and the overview reuse the task list. Opening notes asks for a missing field, so it reads once more. Returning to that detail reuses the new information.

Runs a deterministic simulated source with the real Vem runtime. Interactive controls are available in the HTML page; no JavaScript is needed to read this explanation.

## Render a list and filter

In an application that already uses Vem, import its resource contract (`tasks` here). The application supplies `DataProvider` once; each screen just uses the hooks. If you are connecting a new application, start with [define a resource](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/resources).


```tsx
import { useQuery } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/react";
import { useState } from "react";
import { tasks } from "../task-board/contract.js";
import { ReadStatus } from "./status.js";

export function TaskList() {
	const [openOnly, setOpenOnly] = useState(false);
	const result = useQuery(
		tasks.list({
			select: ["title", "status"],
			where: openOnly ? { status: "open" } : undefined,
		}),
	);
	return (
		<section>
			<label>
				<input
					type="checkbox"
					checked={openOnly}
					onChange={(event) => setOpenOnly(event.target.checked)}
				/>
				To do only
			</label>
			<ReadStatus result={result} />
			<ul>
				{result.rows.map((row) => (
					<li key={row.key}>
						{row.data.title ?? "Title unavailable"} ·{" "}
						{row.data.status ?? "Status unavailable"}
					</li>
				))}
			</ul>
			{result.unresolved.length > 0 && (
				<section aria-label="Match not confirmed">
					<h3>Match not confirmed</h3>
					<ul>
						{result.unresolved.map((row) => (
							<li key={row.key}>
								{row.data.title ?? "Title unavailable"} ·{" "}
								{row.data.status ?? "Status unavailable"}
							</li>
						))}
					</ul>
				</section>
			)}
		</section>
	);
}
```


`openOnly` is ordinary UI state. Changing it changes the query description. Vem reuses known task statuses to answer immediately; a missing field can require a read. Inline descriptions do not need `useMemo`, a cache key, or an effect.

The local `ReadStatus` helper component used in these examples is shown on the [partial-results page](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/partial-results#render-a-useful-status). It explains loading, errors, or incomplete results while leaving known rows visible. `row.key` is the stable React key; `row.data` contains plain selected values.

## Filter text

Describe matching conditions directly in `where`. To search titles **or** notes:


```ts
import { tasks } from "../task-board/contract.js";

export function matchingTasks(text: string) {
	return tasks.list({
		select: ["title", "status"],
		where: text
			? {
					$or: [
						{ title: { contains: text, case: "insensitive" } },
						{ notes: { contains: text, case: "insensitive" } },
					],
				}
			: undefined,
	});
}
```


Pass `matchingTasks(text)` to `useQuery`, or to `client.read` outside React. The query still selects only title and status for display. Vem uses known information first and chooses acquisition when needed; components do not choose a search endpoint or fetch every task's notes.

`contains` matches a literal substring: punctuation such as `.` or `[` is not a pattern. Both case and accents are sensitive by default. This example ignores case but distinguishes `cafe` from `café`; set `accents: "insensitive"` to match both. Case folding is independent of the browser's locale.

Fields in the same object must **all** match. This query selects open tasks whose notes contain “picnic”:


```ts
export const openPicnicTasks = tasks.list({
	select: ["title"],
	where: {
		status: "open",
		notes: { contains: "picnic", case: "insensitive" },
	},
});
```


`$or` requires at least one matching branch; `$and` requires every branch. Both accept arrays of `where` objects and can be nested. Ordinary values express equality, such as `where: { status: "open" }`. The resource contract checks field names and value types, including that `contains` targets a string field.

<details>
<summary>Reusable conditions and exact values</summary>

Use `ResourceFilter<typeof tasks>` for a reusable condition, or `Where<Task>` when you have the resource value type. Filtering by a field does not select it: a query selecting only title cannot access notes through `row.data`. For local presentation choices, `matchesWhere(values, condition)` uses the same comparison rules and returns `true`, `false`, or `"unknown"` when values are missing.

Use `{ eq: value }` for exact object or array equality. This distinguishes a literal object from an operator such as `{ contains: "picnic" }`. An explicit `{ eq: undefined }` matches an established unset value when the field type allows it; it does not match information Vem has not obtained. Similarly, `null` is a value, not a request for missing data.

Query construction rejects malformed operators and undeclared fields before acquisition. Empty `where` objects match every resource; `$and: []` matches every resource and `$or: []` matches none.

</details>

An unknown filter value does not automatically exclude a task. Another `$or` branch or an exact filtered backend response can establish the match. Without enough evidence, the candidate stays in `unresolved`. Backend filtering requires a matching [source capability](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/planning#support-backend-filters); otherwise Vem may acquire broader information and filter locally.

## Read only while a panel is open

A popup can keep its component mounted without keeping its query active:


```tsx
export function TaskSuggestions({ open }: { open: boolean }) {
	const result = useQuery(tasks.list({ select: ["title"] }), { enabled: open });
	if (!open) return null;
	return (
		<section>
			<ReadStatus result={result} />
			<ul>
				{result.rows.map((row) => (
					<li key={row.key}>{row.data.title ?? "Title unavailable"}</li>
				))}
			</ul>
		</section>
	);
}
```


`enabled` defaults to `true`. When false, the hook releases this consumer's demand and returns an unestablished result with no rows, activities, or acquisition. Its `retry()` is a no-op while disabled. Other consumers and shared knowledge remain intact.

Enabling the query reads current shared knowledge immediately. Sufficient cached information renders without a loading interval; missing or stale requirements can start acquisition. A disabled query does not retain a private copy of protected rows.

## Show known data without requesting it

A selection label may use shared knowledge without requiring a read just because it is visible:


```tsx
import { useQuery, useReadStatus } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/react";
import { type TaskRef, tasks } from "../task-board/contract.js";

export function SelectedTaskLabel({ target }: { target: TaskRef }) {
	const result = useQuery(tasks.get(target, { select: ["title"] }), {
		acquire: false,
	});
	return <span>{result.rows[0]?.data.title ?? "Selected task"}</span>;
}
```


`acquire: false` keeps the subscription: permitted values, incoming changes, identity transitions, and access withdrawal still reach the component. It adds no automatic acquisition or sampling. Unknown fields stay unknown, and stale values remain marked as stale. Calling this result's `retry()` explicitly requests information.

Use `enabled: false` when the component should receive nothing; use `acquire: false` when it should follow what is already known. Normal queries acquire automatically.

## Show progress for related reads

Suppose visible task rows each query their own notes. A toolbar can observe that work without requesting notes for every task or registering the rows in a group:


```tsx
export function TaskNotesProgress() {
	const status = useReadStatus(tasks.list({ select: ["notes"] }));
	return (
		<div>
			{status.pending && (
				<progress
					aria-label={
						status.revalidating ? "Checking notes for changes" : "Loading notes"
					}
				/>
			)}
			<div aria-live="polite">
				{status.issues.map((issue) => (
					<p key={`${issue.kind}:${issue.scope}:${issue.message}`}>
						{issue.message}
					</p>
				))}
			</div>
			{status.canRetry && (
				<button type="button" onClick={() => void status.retry()}>
					Try again
				</button>
			)}
		</div>
	);
}
```


Each row still uses an ordinary `useQuery(tasks.get(target, { select: ["notes"] }))`. Vem combines those needs automatically. `useReadStatus` uses its description only to match work by resource, scope, identity, filter, and fields, including work from other tabs sharing the owner.

- `pending` means related work is queued or running. It does not mean every task has notes available.
- `revalidating` means that work is checking stale information; keep existing readable content visible.
- `issues` and `canRetry` describe unsuccessful related acquisition for current consumers. `retry()` retries those queries, including any other information they still need; it does not turn this progress observer into a data request.

Issues leave this status when the relevant demand ends, succeeds, or is withdrawn. This is progress for current reads, not a history of resource failures. `{ enabled: false }` stops the status subscription without affecting those reads.

## Add a column

Select the field, then render it. For example, to show notes:


```tsx
const result = useQuery(tasks.get(target, { select: ["title", "notes"] }));
return result.rows.map((row) => (
	<p key={row.key}>{row.data.notes ?? "Notes unavailable"}</p>
));
```


Unselected fields are TypeScript errors. Selected fields can still be missing from a response, so the example uses a fallback. To perform an operation that requires an actual string, import `hasFields` from `@hyecompany/vem-data` and narrow just what you need:


```tsx
return result.rows.map((row) => (
	<p key={row.key}>
		{hasFields(row, "title")
			? row.data.title.toUpperCase()
			: "Title unavailable"}
	</p>
));
```


`row.complete` narrows all selected fields together. Neither guard turns a proposed value into a confirmed server fact; `row.fields.notes?.source` identifies a proposal when that distinction matters to the UI.

## Open one task

Pass a resource reference such as `{ id: "walk" }` from navigation or a selected row:


```tsx
import { useQuery } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/react";
import { type TaskRef, tasks } from "../task-board/contract.js";
import { ReadStatus } from "./status.js";

export function TaskDetail({ target }: { target: TaskRef }) {
	const result = useQuery(tasks.get(target, { select: ["title", "notes"] }));
	if (result.exists === false) return <p>This task no longer exists.</p>;
	const row = result.rows[0] ?? result.unresolved[0];
	return (
		<section>
			<ReadStatus result={result} />
			{result.rows.length === 0 && row && <p>Match not confirmed</p>}
			{row && (
				<>
					<h2>{row.data.title ?? "Title unavailable"}</h2>
					<p>{row.data.notes ?? "Notes unavailable"}</p>
				</>
			)}
		</section>
	);
}
```


`exists === false` means absence is established. `undefined` means Vem does not know yet. A resource concealed by permissions need not be reported as nonexistent.

When a list also contains proposed creations, only actual resources can be command targets:


```tsx
const row = result.rows[0];
const command =
	row?.identity.kind === "resource"
		? tasks.commands.complete(row.identity.resource)
		: undefined;
```


Next: [bind a command](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/actions) or [handle partial results](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/partial-results).


---

# Partial rows and honest empty states

Keep useful content visible when some information is missing.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/partial-results


A task without a title is still a task. A task without enough evidence to match a “To do” filter stays unresolved. A failed read does not erase the information already on screen.

### Experiment: When part of the list is missing

Choose what the task service returns.

A missing title keeps the matching task visible. A missing filter status leaves a candidate unresolved. A failed read preserves known tasks and offers retry. Only complete empty membership proves that there are no tasks.

Runs a deterministic simulated source with the real Vem runtime. Interactive controls are available in the HTML page; no JavaScript is needed to read this explanation.

## Render a useful status

Use this small companion beside your list or detail. `queryView` chooses the ordinary state with existing content first; the component adds explanations and retry without replacing the rows.


```tsx
import type { QueryResult } from "@hyecompany/vem-data";
import { queryView } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/react";

export function ReadStatus<T extends object, I>({
	result,
}: {
	result: QueryResult<T, I> & { retry(): Promise<QueryResult<T, I>> };
}) {
	const view = queryView(result);
	const message = {
		content: "",
		empty: "No matching tasks.",
		loading: "Loading tasks…",
		restricted: "Some task information is not available to you.",
		error: "Could not finish reading tasks.",
		incomplete: "The complete list is not known yet.",
	}[view];
	const incomplete =
		!result.confirmed.complete ||
		result.rows.some((row) => !row.complete) ||
		result.unresolved.length > 0;
	return (
		<div aria-live="polite">
			{message && <p>{message}</p>}
			{result.revalidating ? (
				<p>Checking for changes…</p>
			) : result.stale ? (
				<p>The last known result could not be confirmed.</p>
			) : result.fetching && view === "content" ? (
				<p>Reading missing information…</p>
			) : null}
			{result.unresolved.length > 0 && (
				<p>Some tasks still need information to match this filter.</p>
			)}
			{result.issues.map((issue) => (
				<p key={`${issue.kind}:${issue.scope}:${issue.message}`}>
					{issue.message}
				</p>
			))}
			{result.settled &&
				!result.empty &&
				(result.issues.some((issue) => issue.kind === "read") ||
					((incomplete || result.stale) && result.issues.length === 0)) && (
					<button type="button" onClick={() => void result.retry()}>
						Try again
					</button>
				)}
		</div>
	);
}
```


Render missing cells with a fallback such as `row.data.title ?? "Title unavailable"`. You do not have to wrap every cell in a special component.

`result.retry()` retries unsuccessful acquisition for this query. It does not grant access or force a refetch of already sufficient information.

## Choose the right count

| You want to show | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Rows the UI can display | `rows` |
| “Some tasks still need checking” | `unresolved.length` |
| “3 confirmed matches so far” | `confirmed.knownCount` |
| “3 tasks total” | `confirmed.total`, only when `confirmed.complete` |
| “No matching tasks” | `empty`, never `rows.length === 0` |

`rows` includes known matches with missing display values and visible action proposals. `unresolved` contains candidates whose filter or scope cannot be evaluated. Do not render those as established matches. A matching `$or` branch or exact filtered backend membership can establish a match even when another filter field is unknown; that does not fill in its missing display value.

A proposed creation is not a confirmed resource and does not inflate the confirmed count. `activities` holds related action progress and outcomes, separate from the rows.

## Keep values visible while checking them

Use `revalidating` for a quiet “Checking for changes…” indication beside retained values. Do not replace them with a loading screen. `stale` says relevant evidence is no longer current; it does not say a read is running.

| State | Presentation |
| --- | --- |
| `revalidating` | Keep available content visible and signal that the result is being checked |
| `stale` without `revalidating` | Keep permitted values visible as last known; explain a failure or stopped check |
| `fetching` without `stale` | Acquire missing information; retain any content already available |
| `settled` with missing information | Show the partial result and its explanation, with retry where useful |

`fetching` covers all active acquisition. `settled` means the current attempt has ended, even if it could not provide everything. Neither a failed check nor an unavailable field calls for an endless spinner.

If a filter or scope is no longer confirmed, the retained candidate belongs in `unresolved`. Show it separately with a label such as **Match not confirmed**; it is not a confirmed match and might never have been one. The [list example](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/display) renders that distinction.

For finer presentation, `row.fields.title?.stale` identifies the affected field. Its `liveness` describes the kind of continuing coverage, not whether a request is active. A plain snapshot is not automatically stale.

A previously empty result can also need checking. It may still contain no rows, but `empty` is false until current evidence proves emptiness again. Show the check status; do not announce “No matching tasks” or invent missing rows.

For why a read happens, continue to [shared knowledge and acquisition](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand/acquisition).


---

# Commands, progress, and outcomes

Add an action button and show what happened.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/actions


Mark the task complete, then choose how the service replies. The checkmark can change before success is known.

### Experiment: A checkmark before confirmation

Complete the walk, then let the task service reply.

A command proposes a completed task while its action awaits a reply. Confirm, reject, save only a note, or lose the reply. Only confirmed success establishes completion; an unknown outcome keeps the preview unconfirmed.

Runs a deterministic simulated source with the real Vem runtime. Interactive controls are available in the HTML page; no JavaScript is needed to read this explanation.

## Add the button

The resource contract names the operation. The command captures its target, so the component does not choose an endpoint or manage an optimistic rollback.


```tsx
import type { ActionHandle } from "@hyecompany/vem-data";
import { useAction, useCommand } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/react";
import { useState } from "react";
import { type TaskRef, tasks } from "../task-board/contract.js";

export function CompleteTask({ target }: { target: TaskRef }) {
	const complete = useCommand(tasks.commands.complete(target));
	const [action, setAction] = useState<ActionHandle>();
	if (action) return <ActionFeedback action={action} onRetry={setAction} />;
	return (
		<div>
			<button
				type="button"
				disabled={!complete.canRun}
				onClick={() => setAction(complete.run())}
			>
				Complete task
			</button>
			{complete.availability.reason && <p>{complete.availability.reason}</p>}
		</div>
	);
}
```


`canRun` means Vem can admit an attempt **now**. A known denial disables the button and supplies a reason. Unknown authorization still permits an attempt; the server can reject it. Admission is checked again when you run.

This completion button keeps the returned handle so it can show feedback in place of the button. Holding a handle observes shared work; it does not create a second operation registry.

## Show progress and the result

`ActionFeedback` uses `useAction` from the same imports above:


```tsx
export function ActionFeedback({
	action,
	onRetry,
}: {
	action: ActionHandle;
	onRetry: (action: ActionHandle) => void;
}) {
	const state = useAction(action);
	const [controlError, setControlError] = useState<string>();
	const outcome = state.outcome;
	const message = !outcome
		? (state.progress?.message ?? "Working…")
		: outcome.kind === "succeeded"
			? "Task completed."
			: outcome.kind === "failed"
				? outcome.error.message
				: outcome.kind === "partial"
					? (outcome.message ?? "Only part of the change was saved.")
					: outcome.message;
	return (
		<div>
			<output>{message}</output>
			{controlError && <p role="alert">{controlError}</p>}
			{state.controls.canRetry && (
				<button type="button" onClick={() => onRetry(action.retry())}>
					Try again
				</button>
			)}
			{state.controls.canCancel && (
				<button
					type="button"
					onClick={async () => {
						try {
							await action.cancel();
						} catch {
							setControlError(
								"Cancellation could not be confirmed. Check the operation before trying again.",
							);
						}
					}}
				>
					Cancel operation
				</button>
			)}
		</div>
	);
}
```


`run()` returns immediately. `useAction` observes the action as it progresses; imperative code can `await action.result`. A domain can supply more specific success or partial values for the feature to render.

| Result | Meaning for your UI |
| --- | --- |
| `succeeded` | The operation completed according to the available evidence |
| `partial` | Some work succeeded; describe that work and what remains |
| `failed` | A failure is known; it may have happened after submission |
| `unknown` | There is not enough evidence to say what happened |

An unknown result is not permission to retry. Show retry only when `controls.canRetry` permits it, and cancellation only when `controls.canCancel` permits it. A partial save must not become “nothing was saved.”

## Let other views follow the change

The definition supplies proposals and confirmed updates. A list using `useQuery` receives them automatically. The feature does not invalidate queries or restore an old snapshot on failure.

### A proposal sits above confirmed facts

1. The service last confirmed this task is open.
2. The component previews completion while the action runs.
3. Events can change the confirmed task beneath the preview.
4. When the preview ends, show current facts, not an old snapshot.

Removing a proposal does not restore a saved old snapshot. Success must be supported by backend evidence; a partial or unknown outcome cannot be rewritten as complete success.

Known updates can arrive while a proposal is visible. Ending that proposal reveals the latest confirmed information. An unknown outcome keeps its proposal labeled unconfirmed; a failed create proposal can also remain for feedback according to the definition.

<details>
<summary>Navigation, feedback, and cancellation</summary>

Removing this component stops its observation. It does not cancel accepted server work. A query's `activities` and `useActivities()` can display shared progress after remounting; the [application feedback layer](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/feedback) handles unsolicited toasts when the feature leaves the screen.

Dismissing a toast acknowledges feedback. Canceling asks the domain to cancel work. A destructive operation such as force-stopping a service is a separate command. These controls should have different labels.

</details>


---

# Build a protected editor

Keep a draft safe while the saved value or permissions change.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/editors


Edit the notes, then try a teammate’s update before saving. Your input should remain yours to resolve.

### Experiment: Keep your own draft

Change the meeting time and save the task.

A managed edit keeps your input with the version it came from. A teammate’s change does not replace your draft. Saving against that older version conflicts. Read-only access keeps readable input; losing notes access removes just the private notes.

Runs a deterministic simulated source with the real Vem runtime. Interactive controls are available in the HTML page; no JavaScript is needed to read this explanation.

## Bind inputs to the managed draft

The `tasks.edits.notes(target)` definition supplies the saved values and the version used for conditional writes. Your component owns the form:


```tsx
import { useEdit } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/react";
import { type TaskRef, tasks } from "../task-board/contract.js";

export function NotesEditor({ target }: { target: TaskRef }) {
	const edit = useEdit(tasks.edits.notes(target));
	const conflict =
		edit.outcome?.kind === "failed" && edit.outcome.error.code === "conflict";
	return (
		<form
			onSubmit={(event) => {
				event.preventDefault();
				if (edit.canSave) edit.save();
			}}
		>
			{Object.hasOwn(edit.values, "notes") && (
				<label>
					Notes
					<textarea
						value={edit.values.notes ?? ""}
						readOnly={edit.status !== "ready"}
						onChange={(event) => edit.set("notes", event.target.value)}
					/>
				</label>
			)}
			{edit.status === "loading" && <p>Reading the saved notes…</p>}
			{edit.reason && <p aria-live="polite">{edit.reason}</p>}
			{edit.outcome?.kind === "failed" && (
				<p role="alert">
					{conflict
						? "The saved notes changed. Your draft is still here."
						: edit.outcome.error.message}
				</p>
			)}
			{edit.outcome?.kind === "unknown" && (
				<p role="alert">{edit.outcome.message}</p>
			)}
			{edit.outcome?.kind === "succeeded" && <output>Saved.</output>}
			<button type="submit" disabled={!edit.canSave}>
				{edit.saving ? "Saving…" : "Save notes"}
			</button>
			<button
				type="button"
				disabled={edit.saving || edit.status === "loading"}
				onClick={() => void edit.reload()}
			>
				Discard draft and reload
			</button>
		</form>
	);
}
```


`edit.set` updates the draft. `edit.save` creates the save action. `canSave` accounts for preparation, dirty state, an active save, and current write access. Add your own validation alongside it.

`Object.hasOwn` is intentional: readable notes can be an empty string, while an unreadable field is removed from `edit.values`. Do not replace an absent protected field with an editable blank input.

## Handle a newer saved version

An **ETag** is the backend’s token for the version you edited. Saving sends your draft with that original token. If someone saved a newer version, this task definition reports `failed` with error code `conflict`.

The hook keeps the draft and disables another save until you establish a new baseline. The example offers **Discard draft and reload**, explicitly naming the loss of input. A richer editor can offer a comparison UI; Vem does not automatically merge text.

### An editor keeps its concurrency baseline

1. Read the saved notes and their version together.
2. Keep typed changes with that original version.
3. A teammate’s update changes shared facts, not dirty input.
4. Send draft + original version. A conflict preserves the draft.

Reload explicitly discards the draft and prepares a new baseline. Known read revocation removes protected values; write-only loss keeps readable values and disables saving.

A successful save prepares a fresh baseline. A partial or uncertain save requires review; it must not be presented as a clean success. Add rendering for any partial outcome declared by your edit contract.

## Keep readable input; remove unreadable input

Write-only loss disables saving while retaining values the user may still read. Losing read access removes the affected baseline and draft fields. Regaining access does not revive the old private draft; reload an authorized baseline.

The component above renders directly from `edit.values`. Copying protected values into `useState`, logs, or form-library defaults makes extra copies that Vem cannot withdraw. If you adopt a form library, its integration must clear both values and default values when fields are withdrawn.

Defining the backend side belongs in [conditional edits](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/commands-edits), not in each form.

A failed reload preserves the permitted draft and reports an error. Unrelated updates do not clear that error or re-enable saving. Retry the reload to establish a writable baseline; access withdrawal still removes unreadable fields while the error is present.


---

# Use Vem outside React

Read, observe, and run commands through the same descriptions.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/imperative


Use the application's existing `DataClient` in a controller or another UI framework. It describes the same information as a React hook; it does not create another owner.

## Read once


```ts
import type { DataClient } from "@hyecompany/vem-data";
import { type TaskRef, tasks } from "../task-board/contract.js";

export async function readTitle(
	client: DataClient,
	target: TaskRef,
	signal: AbortSignal,
) {
	const result = await client.read(tasks.get(target, { select: ["title"] }), {
		signal,
	});
	return {
		title: result.rows[0]?.data.title,
		exists: result.exists,
		issues: result.issues,
	};
}
```


The read settles with available, partial, or failed information after the acquisition attempt. A missing title remains `undefined`; inspect `issues` rather than assuming a complete object. `exists === false` is established absence.

Pass an `AbortSignal` when the caller needs a deadline or can leave the screen. Aborting, closing the client, or using an invalid description can reject the promise; handle those errors at your caller boundary. There is no automatic deadline for an unresponsive source.

## Run an operation


```ts
export async function completeTask(client: DataClient, target: TaskRef) {
	const action = client.run(tasks.commands.complete(target));
	return await action.result;
}
```


The returned outcome has the same success, partial, failure, and uncertainty meanings as [React actions](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/actions). The action handle also provides `subscribe` and `getSnapshot` for progress. Unsubscribing stops observation, not execution.

## Keep a view current

Call this once when the view attaches, and call its returned cleanup when the view leaves:


```ts
export function observeTitles(
	client: DataClient,
	render: (titles: readonly (string | undefined)[]) => void,
) {
	const handle = client.watch(tasks.list({ select: ["title"] }));
	const update = () =>
		render(handle.getSnapshot().rows.map((row) => row.data.title));
	const unsubscribe = handle.subscribe(update);
	update();
	return () => {
		unsubscribe();
		handle.dispose();
	};
}
```


Retry is on the query handle. You do not need a separate refresh query or an event subscription in the view.

Pass `{ acquire: false }` as the second argument to `client.watch` to observe permitted knowledge without requesting missing or stale data. The handle still receives changes and access withdrawal; its explicit `retry()` can acquire.

## Observe read progress without requesting data


```ts
export function observeNoteReads(
	client: DataClient,
	render: (pending: boolean) => void,
) {
	const handle = client.watchReadStatus(tasks.list({ select: ["notes"] }));
	const update = () => render(handle.getSnapshot().pending);
	const unsubscribe = handle.subscribe(update);
	update();
	return () => {
		unsubscribe();
		handle.dispose();
	};
}
```


`watchReadStatus` reports related work from current consumers, including other tabs. Its snapshot has `pending`, `revalidating`, `issues`, and `canRetry`; `handle.retry()` retries unsuccessful matching work. It creates no data demand, and disposing it stops observation without stopping other consumers' reads. See [related read status](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/display#show-progress-for-related-reads) for matching and retry behavior.

<details>
<summary>Writing an editor without React</summary>

`prepareEdit` returns the writable values, matching ETag, and disclosure information. `saveEdit` accepts that prepared representation and the draft. A custom editor must manage the access lifetime of copied values, preserve the original baseline while dirty, and discard it on authority or owner changes. The React `useEdit` binding already supplies that state management; the lower-level pair is not a drop-in form binding.

</details>


---

# Test a feature and its states

Supply data and outcomes without a worker or a backend.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/testing


A feature test should prove what a person sees and can do. `createTestClient` supplies the same provider contract as the application, using named queries, commands, and edits.

## Render an incomplete list

Pass your React test library's `render` function to this helper:


```tsx
import { DataProvider } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/react";
import { createTestClient } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/testing";
import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { tasks } from "../task-board/contract.js";
import { TaskList } from "./list.js";

export function renderPartialList(render: (view: ReactNode) => void) {
	const fixture = createTestClient({
		queries: [
			{
				query: tasks.list({ select: ["title", "status"], where: undefined }),
				rows: [
					{ identity: { id: "walk" }, data: { title: "Plan a weekend walk" } },
				],
				complete: true,
			},
		],
	});
	render(
		<DataProvider client={fixture.client}>
			<TaskList />
		</DataProvider>,
	);
	return fixture;
}
```


Assert that **Plan a weekend walk** is visible with **Status unavailable**. The collection has complete membership, but the row is missing a display field. The component should not hide it or claim the list is empty.

Unmount the view before calling `fixture.close()` in test cleanup. Keep one fixture per test.

## Change the situation while the view is open


```tsx
export function showFailure(fixture: ReturnType<typeof createTestClient>) {
	fixture.setQuery({
		query: tasks.list({ select: ["title", "status"], where: undefined }),
		rows: [
			{ identity: { id: "walk" }, data: { title: "Plan a weekend walk" } },
		],
		status: "failed",
		error: "The task service is unavailable.",
	});
}
```


Call `showFailure(fixture)` after rendering. Assert that the known task remains visible and the source error is shown. Use `setQuery` to supply another result; `replace` lists fields whose old values must be removed when intentionally switching to a partial scenario.

Fixtures match query descriptions. If a test changes the filter, supply a fixture for that filtered query too, or establish sufficient known information for the runtime to answer it.

## Exercise a conflict and access loss


```tsx
export function conflictFixture() {
	const edit = tasks.edits.notes({ id: "walk" });
	const fixture = createTestClient({
		edits: [
			{
				edit,
				values: { notes: "Meet at 10 by the river." },
				etag: '"version-1"',
				outcome: {
					kind: "failed",
					submitted: true,
					error: { code: "conflict", message: "The saved notes changed." },
				},
			},
		],
	});
	return { fixture, edit };
}
```


Render `NotesEditor` inside `DataProvider` using `fixture.client` and target `{ id: "walk" }`. Type a new meeting time and save. Assert that the conflict appears and the typed value remains.

Then withdraw just the notes:


```tsx
export function hideNotes({
	fixture,
	edit,
}: ReturnType<typeof conflictFixture>) {
	fixture.setEditAccess(edit, { fields: { notes: "denied" } });
}
```


Assert that the textarea and its value disappear. For write-only loss, use `setEditAccess(edit, { write: "denied" })` and assert that Save is disabled while readable input stays.

## Choose the boundary to test

| Change | Useful check |
| --- | --- |
| A field or filter | Type-check selected fields; render missing values |
| A command | Admission, progress, and command-specific outcomes |
| An editor | Dirty external change, conflict, and access loss |
| A domain definition | Real backend responses, events, and replacement boundaries |
| A browser host | Actual worker ownership, two tabs, and storage failures |

Feature fixtures exercise the runtime's consumer behavior, not HTTP, IndexedDB, or worker ownership. Those belong in integration tests. For manual exploration inside an application, see [development tools](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/devtools).


---

# Connect your data

Give Vem your backend rules once; keep feature code small.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect


This section is for the person integrating a backend. If a resource already exists, go straight to [Build with Vem](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build).

Start with one resource and its available reads. Add the other pieces as the application needs them:

| Your next task | Guide |
| --- | --- |
| Turn a backend response into usable rows | [Define a resource](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/resources) |
| Show private data to the right caller | [Implement access controls](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/access) |
| Keep views in sync with events | [Events, relationships, and derived values](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/events) |
| Save changes or run an operation | [Commands and conditional edits](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/commands-edits) |
| Share the owner across browser tabs | [Browser host](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/browser-host) |
| Keep progress visible after navigation | [Shared feedback](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/feedback) |
| Exercise loading, failures, and permissions | [Development tools](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/devtools) |

Vem plans automatically from your source declarations. Persistence and development panels are separate host choices.

To describe bulk reads, filtering, pagination, and optional backend cost models, see [how Vem chooses reads](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/planning). For accepted background jobs, [observe and recover an operation](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/operations). These extend the first adapter without changing feature code.


---

# Connect a resource

Teach Vem how your backend supplies one kind of data.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/resources


A feature asks for tasks. Your integration describes the available backend reads and what each response provides. Vem chooses among them for the whole application’s outstanding needs.

This guide assumes a task API with two endpoints: `GET /api/tasks` returns **every task and all its fields**; `GET /api/tasks/:id` returns one task. A backend with pagination or brief list representations needs different coverage rules, explained below.

## Give features a contract

The contract names the fields, identity, commands, and editors that components can use. Constructing any of these descriptions performs no work.


```ts
import {
	defineCommand,
	defineEdit,
	defineResource,
} from "@hyecompany/vem-data";

export interface Task {
	title: string;
	status: "open" | "done";
	notes: string;
}
export interface TaskRef {
	id: string;
}
export interface Notes {
	notes: string;
}
export const tasks = defineResource<Task, TaskRef>()({
	name: "tasks",
	fields: ["title", "status", "notes"],
	defaultSelect: ["title", "status"],
	commands: { complete: defineCommand<void, { kind: "succeeded" }>() },
	edits: { notes: defineEdit<Notes, { kind: "succeeded" }>() },
});
```


The command and editor names are declarations; [their implementations](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/commands-edits) come after the read adapter. Keep the contract in a module features can import. The HTTP adapter belongs in the owner, where credentials and transport are available.

## Separate read rules from transport

The task example needs only a name and a public read permission:


```ts
import type { ResourceReadDefinition } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/client";

export const taskRead: ResourceReadDefinition = {
	name: "tasks",
	access: "public",
};
```


Here `ResourceReadDefinition` is imported from `@hyecompany/vem-data/client`. Install these same pure rules in the owner and each tab. Vem evaluates typed `where` conditions, including their required fields when deciding whether a row matches. [Text and combined filters](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/display#filter-text) need no custom matcher.

<details>
<summary>Project scopes and advanced matching</summary>

Add `inScope` when a collection has project or tenant boundaries. A resource identity must distinguish otherwise identical names in different projects.

Most resources need no custom matcher. If your integration overrides equality matching with `matches`, it receives normalized equality maps, including equivalent `$and` conditions. List additional fields it reads in `queryDependencies` and return `"unknown"` when those inputs are absent. Vem evaluates the remaining normalized filter expressions itself.

</details>

## Declare sources and extract their evidence

Describe each representation once. `fields` identifies its information; `membership: true` says a list can establish which tasks exist. Vem chooses when to call `run`:


```ts
import type { ResourceDefinition } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime";
import type { TaskRef } from "../task-board/contract.js";
import { taskRead } from "../task-board/read.js";

export const taskAdapter: ResourceDefinition = {
	...taskRead,
	sources: [
		{
			key: "all-tasks",
			mode: "list",
			fields: ["title", "status", "notes"],
			membership: true,
			async run(_request, context) {
				const records: TaskRecord[] = await readTasks("", context.signal);
				return {
					facts: records.map(taskFact),
					memberships: [
						{
							resource: "tasks",
							identities: records.map(({ id }) => ({ id })),
							complete: true,
							basis: ["public"],
						},
					],
				};
			},
		},
		{
			key: "one-task",
			mode: "one",
			fields: ["title", "status", "notes"],
			async run(request, context) {
				const path = `/${encodeURIComponent((request.identity as TaskRef).id)}`;
				const record: TaskRecord = await readTasks(path, context.signal);
				return { facts: [taskFact(record)] };
			},
		},
	],
};
```


Each `key` names a backend source within this resource. It is not a query cache key; components describe their needs without defining keys.

This complete owner definition imports the contract and read rules above. `TaskRef` is `{ id: string }`; `TaskRecord` is the backend response with that ID plus the contract's task fields. The cast at the adapter boundary uses this resource's identity type. Validate external response shapes in your transport when they are not already checked.

The transport checks HTTP success, and `taskFact` extracts one response:


```ts
import type { FactObservation } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime";
import type { Task } from "../task-board/contract.js";

interface TaskRecord extends Task {
	id: string;
}
async function readTasks(path: string, signal: AbortSignal) {
	const response = await fetch(`/api/tasks${path}`, { signal });
	if (!response.ok)
		throw new Error(`Task service returned HTTP ${response.status}`);
	return response.json();
}
function taskFact(task: TaskRecord): FactObservation {
	return {
		resource: "tasks",
		identity: { id: task.id },
		values: { title: task.title, status: task.status, notes: task.notes },
		presence: "present",
		basis: ["public"],
	};
}
```


Returning a batch lets the runtime apply it through the acquisition's context. For an intermediate update, use `context.observe(batch)`. Do not start a fetch and later call a global `runtime.observe`: that loses the request's protection against obsolete responses.

| Your response establishes… | Report… |
| --- | --- |
| Some fields of a task | A fact with those `values` |
| The tasks seen on one page | Membership with `complete: false` |
| The entire matching collection | Membership with `complete: true`, for its actual scope and filter |
| One task's details | Its facts; no claim about the whole collection |

Missing display fields keep a known task visible. Unknown filter fields keep a candidate unresolved unless other evidence, such as exact filtered membership, establishes the match. If a successful response cannot provide everything, return what it does establish; reads settle partial. Throw on an acquisition failure so the result can explain it and offer retry.

<details>
<summary>When omission means deletion</summary>

`replace` names a representation's fields whose omission means removal. A brief list response must not delete notes that only appear in details. Report `presence: "absent"` only when absence is established; a concealed resource or generic permission error does not prove deletion.

</details>

## Install the definition

Give `taskAdapter` to the owner's `resources` array and `taskRead` to the tab's read definitions. The [browser-host guide](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/browser-host) shows that connection. Components continue importing `tasks` from the contract; adding a field does not add a fetch effect.

The [automatic planning guide](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/planning) explains how these declarations combine across views and tabs, including costs, filters, and pages. For live updates, continue to [events](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/events). For protected data, [connect permissions](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/access).


---

# Apply events and derive values

Update shared information from what the backend actually tells you.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/events


If the backend announces that a task is done, every view can use that fact immediately. The adapter translates the event once; components do not subscribe to the event stream or invalidate their queries.

## Publish a value from an event

Add this function as `event: taskStatusEvent` on the task's owner definition. It accepts a small event with an ID and the new status:


```ts
import type { ResourceDefinition } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime";

export const taskStatusEvent: ResourceDefinition["event"] = (value) => {
	if (
		typeof value !== "object" ||
		value === null ||
		!("id" in value) ||
		typeof value.id !== "string" ||
		!("status" in value) ||
		(value.status !== "open" && value.status !== "done")
	) {
		throw new Error("Invalid task status event");
	}
	return {
		facts: [
			{
				resource: "tasks",
				identity: { id: value.id },
				values: { status: value.status },
				basis: ["public"],
				liveness: { channel: "task-status" },
			},
		],
	};
};
```


`ResourceDefinition` comes from `@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime`. The validator rejects malformed input. It publishes only the status: it does not pretend this event supplied the task's title, notes, or a complete list.

In the owner, route the transport's decoded messages to that definition:


```ts
import type { Runtime } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime";

export function connectedTaskEvents(runtime: Runtime) {
	runtime.setContinuity({ channel: "task-status" }, "live");
}
export function receiveTaskStatus(runtime: Runtime, payload: unknown) {
	runtime.event("tasks", payload);
}
export function lostTaskEvents(runtime: Runtime) {
	runtime.setContinuity({ channel: "task-status" }, "interrupted");
}
```


`Runtime` is imported from the same entry point. Connect `receiveTaskStatus` to decoded events. Call `connectedTaskEvents` only when delivery is continuous for that channel, and `lostTaskEvents` on an interruption. A channel is a named continuity guarantee, not merely an open socket. If a subscription covers only one project, include that project in the channel reference's `scope`.

| The event contains… | The adapter should… |
| --- | --- |
| A new field value | Publish that fact directly |
| Proof a resource was deleted | Publish `presence: "absent"` |
| Only “this field changed” | Mark that specific evidence unsupported so an active reader can acquire it |
| An unknown span of missed changes | Mark the affected channel and scope interrupted |

The last two cases acknowledge missing evidence. They are not a reason to periodically reread ordinary data. An update event cannot prove that an enumeration is complete.

## Declare which fields the events keep current

### Experiment: Different fields, different guarantees

Go offline, change the service, then reconnect. Keep the reply pending, return an error, or confirm the new title.

The real runtime receives an immutable task ID, a title supported by a scoped event channel, and a temperature snapshot. Losing continuity makes the title stale and triggers an unsuccessful targeted read while the simulated service is offline. A service change does not silently update the disconnected view. Reconnecting starts a held check while the old title stays visible. The user can return an error: the title remains last known and the checking indication stops. Retrying and accepting the reply establishes the new title. The ID stays immutable and the old temperature remains a snapshot without automatic polling.

Runs a deterministic simulated source with the real Vem runtime. Interactive controls are available in the HTML page; no JavaScript is needed to read this explanation.

Suppose this backend emits every task-status change, but no title or notes changes. Describe that difference on each acquired representation:


```ts
import type { FactObservation } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime";
import type { TaskRecord } from "../task-board/domain.js";

export function taskWithStatusEvents(task: TaskRecord): FactObservation {
	return {
		resource: "tasks",
		identity: { id: task.id },
		values: { title: task.title, status: task.status, notes: task.notes },
		presence: "present",
		basis: ["public"],
		fieldLiveness: { status: { channel: "task-status" } },
	};
}
```


Use this extraction in the task sources when the status subscription is installed. `fieldLiveness` overrides the observation's default for those fields. For directly observed values, unlisted fields remain snapshots: reading status events does not make notes current.

| Observation declares… | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `liveness: "snapshot"`, or omitted | The value was observed; ongoing change coverage is not established |
| `liveness: { channel, scope? }` | This value relies on that channel's continuous delivery |
| `liveness: "immutable"` | The field genuinely cannot change for this identity |

Use `{ all: [...] }` when several channels are needed, or `{ any: [...] }` for independently sufficient coverage. These expressions describe continuity; permission expressions answer a separate question.

<details>
<summary>When events reveal some changes but cannot cover every change</summary>

Use `liveness: { all: [{ channel: "task-events" }, "snapshot"] }`. The snapshot requirement prevents a false `live` claim, while the channel still records useful change coverage. A known interruption makes affected evidence stale because an event may have been missed. Plain `"snapshot"` declares no such channel dependency.

</details>

A real interruption makes facts that rely on that channel stale. Unrelated fields and independently sufficient coverage survive. Reads made during the interruption still provide useful snapshots. Reconnecting does not retroactively cover missed changes: affected active consumers acquire new evidence. An unchanged, unmonitored snapshot does not gain a TTL or a mount/focus verification policy.

Keep permitted values on screen during repair. `result.revalidating` signals an active check of stale evidence; `result.stale` remains true if the check stops or fails. [Read presentation](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/build/partial-results#keep-values-visible-while-checking-them) shows the shared status component.

The runtime exposes `row.fields.status?.liveness` as `"live"`, `"snapshot"`, or `"immutable"`; `stale` separately reports known missing currency evidence. `live` applies to that field's declared support. It is not a claim that every field or project is monitored.

## Follow a proven rename

A name can be reused. When the backend explicitly connects an old identity to a new one, publish that connection as identity-transition evidence alongside any values the event establishes.

This example uses `ObservationBatch` from `@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime`. The host must have established the `projects:events` disclosure permission and continuous `project-events` delivery.


```ts
export function projectRenamed(
	oldName: string,
	name: string,
): ObservationBatch {
	return {
		identityTransitions: [
			{
				resource: "projects",
				from: { name: oldName },
				to: { name },
				basis: ["projects:events"],
				liveness: { channel: "project-events" },
			},
		],
		facts: [
			{
				resource: "projects",
				identity: { name },
				values: { name },
				basis: ["projects:events"],
				liveness: { channel: "project-events" },
			},
		],
	};
}
```


The transition atomically establishes the old identity's absence and the new identity's presence. It does not copy field values, grants, actions, or edit sessions. Reading the destination still uses its own access requirements.

A detail result exposes `incarnation`, an opaque token for the identity currently known under that name, and `identityTransitions`, explicit connections from former incarnations. The transition remains available when the old identity has no result row.

Capture the token when the user selects a resource. A shared navigation boundary can follow only a transition matching that captured token:


```ts
export function followSelectedProject(
	selected: { identity: ProjectRef; incarnation: string },
	result: QueryResult<{ name: string }, ProjectRef>,
) {
	// Capture selected.incarnation from the row or detail when the user selects it.
	const transition = result.identityTransitions?.find(
		(entry) => entry.from.incarnation === selected.incarnation,
	);
	return transition?.to ?? selected;
}
```


Here `QueryResult` comes from `@hyecompany/vem-data`, and `ProjectRef` is `{ name: string }`. The boundary owns selection; the picker just displays it. Rename chains resolve to the last supported destination.

**Do not match by name alone.** A newly created project with an old name has a different token. Missing events or withdrawn evidence can also end identity continuity. Keep the selected scope and report uncertainty when no matching proof survives; never infer a rename from list differences.

Transition history is bounded and session-local, not a permanent alias or a persisted redirect. A fresh selection observes the current identity rather than replaying former renames. An action already created for an old reference remains targeted there.

## Derive a value from known facts

Suppose every screen uses a human-readable status label. Define it once instead of storing an unrelated copy:


```ts
export const deriveTaskLabel: ResourceDefinition["derive"] = (
	changed,
	context,
) => ({
	facts: changed
		.filter(
			(ref) =>
				"field" in ref && ref.resource === "tasks" && ref.field === "status",
		)
		.flatMap((ref) => {
			const task = context.get("tasks", ref.identity);
			if (!task || !Object.hasOwn(task.values, "status")) return [];
			return [
				{
					resource: "tasks",
					identity: ref.identity,
					values: {
						statusLabel: task.values.status === "done" ? "Completed" : "To do",
					},
					dependsOn: [ref],
				},
			];
		}),
});
```


Install this as `derive: deriveTaskLabel`. Add `statusLabel` to the public contract before selecting it in a component. `changed` identifies evidence that changed; `context.get` reads what is now known. `dependsOn` connects the derived label to its source status, so withdrawal or invalidation of that support affects the label too.

To let Vem acquire the inputs when a consumer asks for the derived field, declare its prerequisites:


```ts
export const taskDependencies: ResourceDefinition["fieldDependencies"] = {
	statusLabel: (identity) => [
		{
			kind: "query",
			resource: "tasks",
			mode: "one",
			identity,
			select: ["status"],
		},
	],
	labelCount: (identity) => [
		{ resource: "tasks", identity, relationship: "labels" },
	],
};
```


Install this as `fieldDependencies: taskDependencies`. The `labelCount` entry is used by the relationship example below. These callbacks describe required information; Vem selects the sources and shares their work with other consumers.

A derived field automatically inherits the currency of every required `dependsOn` fact and relationship. An explicit liveness requirement can add support requirements, but cannot make an unsupported dependency current.

For ordinary formatting used by only one component, a local formatting function is enough. A domain derivation is useful when multiple readers need the same meaning or it participates in queries.

## Record a relationship when links matter

A task's labels are links to label resources, separate from the labels' names or colors:


```ts
import type { ObservationBatch } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime";
import type { TaskRef } from "../task-board/contract.js";

export function taskLabels(
	task: TaskRef,
	labelIds: readonly string[],
): ObservationBatch {
	return {
		relationships: [
			{
				resource: "tasks",
				identity: task,
				relationship: "labels",
				targets: labelIds.map((id) => ({
					resource: "labels",
					identity: { id },
				})),
				complete: true,
				basis: ["public"],
			},
		],
	};
}
```


Here `TaskRef` is `{ id: string }`; `ObservationBatch` comes from `@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime`. Return this batch from acquisition or an event definition. Set `complete: true` only if `labelIds` is the full set. A partial response uses `false`; explicit removals use `removed`.

<details>
<summary>When individual links have different permissions</summary>

Suppose a task links to labels that require different read permissions. Use `targetBasis` to protect each link separately. This example assumes those permissions were verified and the response establishes the entire visible set:


```ts
export function protectedTaskLabels(
	task: TaskRef,
	labels: readonly { id: string; readScope: string }[],
	removedLabelIds: readonly string[] = [],
): ObservationBatch {
	const target = (id: string) => ({ resource: "labels", identity: { id } });
	return {
		relationships: [
			{
				resource: "tasks",
				identity: task,
				relationship: "labels",
				targets: labels.map((label) => target(label.id)),
				targetBasis: labels.map((label) => ({
					target: target(label.id),
					basis: [{ all: ["tasks:read-labels", label.readScope] }],
				})),
				removed: removedLabelIds.map(target),
				complete: true,
				basis: ["tasks:read-labels"],
			},
		],
	};
}
```


Withdrawing one label’s permission removes that link and the claim that the set is complete; other permitted links survive. A count or other value derived from the complete set loses its supporting evidence too. If you also publish all label IDs as one scalar array, protect that aggregate with every permission it requires.

A complete response replaces claims with the same disclosure basis; independently supported links can remain. Populate `removedLabelIds` only when the backend establishes those links were removed. `removed` withdraws the link itself, including independent claims; a partial response or a concealed target does not establish removal.

</details>

To expose the number of labels as an ordinary selected field, derive it only when the set is complete:


```ts
export const deriveLabelCount: ResourceDefinition["derive"] = (
	changed,
	context,
) => ({
	facts: changed.flatMap((ref) => {
		if (
			!("relationship" in ref) ||
			ref.resource !== "tasks" ||
			ref.relationship !== "labels"
		)
			return [];
		const labels = context.relationship("tasks", ref.identity, "labels");
		if (!labels?.complete || labels.stale) return [];
		return [
			{
				resource: "tasks",
				identity: ref.identity,
				values: { labelCount: labels.targets.length },
				dependsOn: [
					{ resource: "tasks", identity: ref.identity, relationship: "labels" },
				],
			},
		];
	}),
});
```


Install this as the resource's `derive` function and add `labelCount: number` to `Task` plus `"labelCount"` to the contract's `fields`. A component can then select `"labelCount"` through its usual task query. If you also use the status-label derivation above, combine their returned facts in the one `derive` function.

A relationship source advertises `relationships: ["labels"]` in its capabilities. The response above establishes the actual links.

To derive label names, register a `labels` resource with its own sources and declare the related information needed:


```ts
export const labelNameDependencies: ResourceDefinition["fieldDependencies"] = {
	labelNames(identity, context) {
		const link = { resource: "tasks", identity, relationship: "labels" };
		const labels = context.relationship("tasks", identity, "labels");
		return [
			link,
			...(labels?.targets ?? []).map((target) => ({
				kind: "query" as const,
				resource: target.resource,
				mode: "one" as const,
				identity: target.identity,
				select: ["name"],
			})),
		];
	},
};
```


Vem first acquires unknown links, then reevaluates the prerequisites and chooses reads for the related names alongside all other demand. A corresponding `labelNames` derivation must depend on both the relationship and those name facts; it publishes a value only when the needed evidence is available. The component still selects an ordinary field.

Next: [implement commands and edits](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/commands-edits).


---

# Implement commands and edits

Turn a feature's intent into an operation with an honest outcome.

URL: https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/commands-edits


The feature says “complete this task.” The domain definition decides whether to admit that attempt, how to send it, and what the reply proves. Put command definitions in the resource's `commands` object; the names match the public contract.

## Complete a task

This command talks to a synchronous endpoint that returns the updated task:


```ts
complete: {
	access: "public",
	disclosure: "public",
	availability(command, context) {
		const known = context.get("tasks", command.target);
		return known?.values.status === "done" && !known.fields.status?.stale
			? { state: "blocked", reason: "This task is already complete." }
			: { state: "available" };
	},
	project: (command) => [
		{
			resource: "tasks",
			identity: command.target,
			kind: "update",
			values: { status: "done" },
		},
	],
	async run(command, context) {
		context.progress({ message: "Completing task…" });
		const response = await request(
			`/${encodeURIComponent((command.target as TaskRef).id)}/complete`,
			context,
			{ method: "POST" },
		);
		context.observe({ facts: [taskFact(await record(response))] });
		return { kind: "succeeded" };
	},
},
```


`TaskRef` is the contract's `{ id: string }` identity. `request` sends an HTTP request with `context.signal`; `record` checks the status and decodes the returned task; `taskFact` extracts its fields as shown in [connecting a resource](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/resources#declare-sources-and-extract-their-evidence).

The transport helpers used above are small. `ResourceContext` is imported from `@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime`; `TaskRecord` has the task fields plus its ID:


```ts
async function fetchTask(
	path: string,
	context: ResourceContext,
	init?: RequestInit,
) {
	return fetch(`/api/tasks${path}`, { ...init, signal: context.signal });
}
async function record(response: Response): Promise<TaskRecord> {
	if (!response.ok)
		throw new Error(`Task source returned HTTP ${response.status}.`);
	return response.json();
}
```


The definition is built by `createTaskDefinition(request = fetchTask)`, so its `request` calls use this helper unless the host supplies another transport. Keep the helpers beside the resource definition; feature components do not call them.

The three parts have distinct jobs:

- `availability` blocks an attempt when current, non-stale evidence says it is already done. Server authorization still applies.
- `project` supplies a temporary preview. It does not establish success or replace the confirmed value.
- `run` sends the operation, publishes confirmed response facts, and reports its outcome. A status event can update the same facts without extra feature code.

These task examples are public. For protected operations, declare `access` with the write permission and `disclosure` with the permissions needed to show the activity. The [permissions guide](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/access) explains how those expressions compose.

## Report what actually happened

| Evidence | Outcome |
| --- | --- |
| The intended work completed | `succeeded` |
| Some work completed and some did not | `partial`, with a value identifying each result |
| The backend definitively rejected or failed the operation | `failed` |
| The request may have succeeded, but the reply is missing | `unknown` |

The runtime records possible submission before calling `run` when persistence works. The synchronous example holds its submission slot until it settles. `context.submitted()` releases that slot early; it does not prove that the backend accepted the operation. For asynchronous APIs, release that slot when submission is acknowledged and then monitor the accepted operation. Publish meaningful progress with `context.progress`.

A thrown error from a mutation becomes `unknown`: a dropped connection cannot prove that no work occurred. Return a definite failure only when your backend's semantics establish it. `submitted: false` means the request did not reach the backend; it must not be used merely because the response was lost.

If your backend returns an accepted job instead of a completed task, continue to [observe and recover a server operation](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/operations). That guide shows the checkpoint, monitoring, and recovery code separately.


## Declare an HTTP upload

Use `transfer` in place of `run` for a file upload. The definition prepares one request and interprets its receipt; Vem manages submission, progress, cancellation, and recovery on the existing action.

This example adds an attachment to a task. **Its backend contract is illustrative:** `PUT` returns HTTP 204 only after the complete attachment is saved. Add an `upload: defineCommand<{ file: File }, { kind: "succeeded" }>()` entry to the task's public command contract, and install `attachmentUpload(apiOrigin)` as its owner definition:


```ts
import type { CommandDefinition } from "@hyecompany/vem-data/runtime";
import type { TaskRef } from "../task-board/contract.js";

export function attachmentUpload(apiOrigin: string): CommandDefinition {
	return {
		access: "public",
		disclosure: "public",
		transfer: {
			prepare(command) {
				const target = command.target as TaskRef;
				const { file } = command.input as { file: File };
				return {
					url: new URL(
						`/api/tasks/${encodeURIComponent(target.id)}/attachments/${encodeURIComponent(file.name)}`,
						apiOrigin,
					).href,
					method: "PUT",
					body: file,
					credentials: "same-origin",
				};
			},
			complete(receipt) {
				if (receipt.kind === "unknown") return receipt;
				return receipt.status === 204
					? { kind: "succeeded" }
					: {
							kind: "unknown",
							message:
								"The service did not confirm that the complete attachment was saved.",
						};
			},
		},
	};
}
```


The component binds `useCommand(tasks.commands.upload(target, { file }))` after a file is selected. It does not manage worker messages or a second operation registry. The example is public like the task board; use your application's write permission for `access` and readable activity permission for `disclosure` when the destination is protected.

`prepare` runs for a new attempt. `complete` interprets a captured response and may run again during recovery, so it must not send another mutation. It can publish established facts with `context.observe`. If HTTP acceptance starts a separate server operation, interpret and monitor that operation rather than treating acceptance as completion.

The built-in host supports `POST`, `PUT`, and `PATCH` uploads with `Blob` bodies. Response text is limited to 64 KiB in UTF-8 and response headers to 16 KiB of encoded JSON; an incomplete or oversized response leaves the result unknown. This is for upload receipts, not downloading arbitrary binary files. Upload bytes and request credentials are not copied into the action journal.

[Configure the browser host](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/connect/browser-host#let-the-browser-continue-an-upload) to enable browser-owned execution. Otherwise the owner sends the request and the UI must explain that an application tab needs to remain open. See [recovery limits](https://hyevem.com/docs/data/understand/recovery#uploads-and-background-transfers) before promising resumption or retry.

## Acquire a writable baseline
